title: The bland Tao
hook: music and fine food stop travelers, but the Tao is bland and never runs out (Tao Te Ching 35)

segments.voice: Yesterday, flowing everywhere: the great Tao feeding everything and claiming none of it. Your line was claim nothing. Did you manage one good thing with no name on it? Day one thousand ninety-seven.

Onions frying at a street fair. A band warming up by the food trucks. People who were walking somewhere else slow down, drift over, and stand there for a while with paper plates. An hour later they're gone, off to the next thing, and the band is packing up. Then, at home that night, somebody drinks a plain glass of water at the kitchen sink. Nobody photographs it. Nobody drifts over to watch. Chapter thirty-five of the Tao Te Ching sets those two scenes side by side, and it makes a surprising claim about which one lasts.
screen: `ONIONS AND A BAND AT A STREET FAIR.` → `A PLAIN GLASS OF WATER.` → `WHICH ONE LASTS?`

segments.voice: First, the great image. The chapter says that whoever holds the great image of the Tao, the whole world comes to them. And those who come find no harm there, only rest, peace and ease. Not excitement. Ease. Second, the street fair. In James Legge's translation: "Music and dainties will make the passing guest stop (for a time)." Dainties is an old word for treats. Notice the chapter doesn't condemn them. Music is good. Treats are good. They really do stop people. But the guest is passing, and the stop is for a time. Third, the bland part. The chapter says the Tao, when it's put into words, seems flat and has no flavor. Look at it, and it doesn't seem worth looking at. Listen, and it doesn't seem worth hearing. That's an odd thing for a book about the Tao to say about the Tao. It doesn't try to sell it. Fourth, the turn. After all that, the chapter's last words, in Legge's version: "the use of it is inexhaustible." The music ends. The plate gets empty. The plain thing never runs out. Back at the street fair, the chapter isn't against any of it: loud, salty, bright, gone by evening. It just sets the plain thing beside it. The chapter names no examples, but some readers think of the plain things nobody would post. Water. Sleep. A walk. The same friend, again.
screen: `THE WORLD COMES, AND FINDS EASE.` · `MUSIC AND TREATS STOP THE PASSING GUEST.` · `THE TAO SEEMS FLAT AND FLAVORLESS.` · `ITS USE NEVER RUNS OUT.` · then, large: `THE USE OF IT IS INEXHAUSTIBLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: enjoy one plain taste. If there's water nearby, take a sip and hold it in your mouth for a moment before you swallow. If not, notice the plain taste already in your mouth, or the plain feeling of air coming in through your nose. Don't look for anything special. The point is the absence of special. Stay with something that has almost no flavor, and see how much is there anyway: coolness, weight, the swallow, the breath after. The bell holds the time.
The bland Tao. Chapter thirty-five's claim that the Tao, put into words, seems flavorless and not worth a look, and yet its use never runs out. Today's word.
Your line: bland and endless. Pick one plain thing in your day, a glass of water, a familiar walk, and give it the attention you'd give a treat. Day one thousand ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter thirty-five as an invitation to value plain, ordinary things, which seem dull beside entertainment and treats but do not run out.

fork.setup: you're a traveler on the road. there's music at an inn and food on the fire. what does chapter thirty-five say happens?
options: you stop there for a while.
fork.reveal: music and dainties make the passing guest stop, for a time. the guest moves on; the plain Tao is the thing that doesn't run out.

original.note: Chinese: plain, thin, weak in flavor; chapter thirty-five's word for how the Tao tastes.

trapdoor: what you thought: calling the Tao bland is an insult.
what it means: next to music and treats the Tao seems flavorless, and unlike them it never runs out.
what a scholar hears: the chapter says the Tao is 淡, plain, and 無味, without flavor; chapter sixty-three turns this into advice to taste the tasteless.

sources.quoted: Music and dainties will make the passing guest stop (for a time).
the use of it is inexhaustible.

sources.ref: Tao Te Ching 35 (the great image; rest, peace and ease; flavorless, not worth looking at or listening to)

notes: Check both Legge 1891 quotations of chapter 35 word for word, including '(for a time)'.

Paraphrases of chapter 35: the world resorts to whoever holds the Great Image and finds no hurt but rest, peace and ease; the Tao as it comes from the mouth seems insipid and without flavor, not worth looking at or listening to. Confirm.
Trapdoor ties 淡 and 無味 in chapter 35 to chapter 63's 味無味 ('taste the tasteless'); confirm.
The closing line of the teach ('the things that hold a life together tend to be the ones nobody would post') is the writer's application, not the text's claim.

Editor pass: the teach had credited the chapter with saying 'the things that hold a life together tend to be the ones nobody would post'; that is now framed as some readers' application, and the chapter is said to name no examples. Replaced the stock 'ordinary Tuesday' turn.
